checks.claim: Key: roots take in water and minerals from the soil
checks.note: 'A primary role of roots is the absorption of water and essential nutrients from the soil'.

checks.claim: Stem: roots anchor the plant firmly
checks.note: 'anchoring them firmly in the soil'.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Make food from sunlight' (roots under the soil do not photosynthesize; leaves do)
checks.note: Page contrasts roots with the photosynthetic shoot; the stem places the roots under the soil, so the rare green aerial roots (orchids) do not make this defensible.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Make seeds for new plants' (flowers make seeds)
checks.note: Some roots support vegetative propagation (root cuttings, suckers), but no root makes seeds; the choice stays wrong as worded.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Draw insects to the flowers' (petals, scent and nectar do)
Context: water and minerals taken in mostly through fine root hairs that give a far bigger surface
checks.note: 'In roots, most water absorption happens through the root hairs'; Grokipedia Root: root hairs 'dramatically increase the root's absorptive surface area'.

checks.claim: Context: minerals are not food; food is made in the leaves; flowers with bright petals draw insects and make the seeds
checks.note: Leaf is 'the primary photosynthetic organ'; a grade-5 simplification that holds.

checks.claim: Key: xylem carries the dyed water up the stem to the petals
checks.note: White carnation in coloured water; water rises through 'millions of tiny tubes called xylem'; results after a few hours, full effect overnight, so 'a day later' is safe.

checks.claim: Xylem carries water and dissolved minerals from roots up to shoots and leaves; made of hollow tubular cells
checks.note: 'unidirectional transport of water and dissolved minerals from roots to shoots and leaves'; 'elongated, tubular cells that die at maturity to form hollow conduits'.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Phloem' (carries sugar from leaves to other parts)
checks.note: 'primarily sugars and other photosynthetic products, from source regions such as leaves to sink regions including roots'.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Stomata' (pores in the leaf, not tubes in the stem)
Wrong: 'Chlorophyll' (green pigment that captures light, not a tube)
Context: phloem carries sugar made in the leaves to the rest of the plant; stomata are tiny pores in the leaves; chlorophyll is the green colouring that catches light
Stem: stomata are tiny pores, more of them on the leaf's underside, each opened and closed by two guard cells
checks.note: 'microscopic pore located in the epidermis of leaves'; 'two kidney-shaped guard cells that control its aperture'; 'predominantly distributed on the abaxial (lower) surface'. Wikipedia Stoma: dicots usually have more below; most trees have them only below.

checks.claim: Key: stomata let gases in and out (CO2 in; oxygen and water vapour out)
checks.note: 'passes through stomata by gaseous diffusion'; 'Water vapour diffuses through the stomata into the atmosphere as part of a process called transpiration'.

checks.claim: Context: stomata close in dry weather to save water
checks.note: 'close during drought to conserve water'.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Sunlight' (light passes through the clear epidermis; no pore needed)
checks.note: Epidermis 'is usually transparent' and its ordinary cells lack chloroplasts.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Minerals' (come up from the roots in the xylem)
Wrong: 'Sugar' (travels in the phloem)
Stem: a bumblebee drinks nectar and pollen clings to its furry body
checks.note: 'Adult bumblebees feed on nectar'; 'The body is densely covered in branched setae forming a pile'; 'transfer pollen via branched body hairs during visitation'. USDA: pollen grains 'attach themselves to the animal's body' while it sips nectar.

checks.claim: Stem: pollen reaching another flower of that kind lets it make seeds
checks.note: 'Seeds can only be produced when pollen is transferred between flowers of the same species'.

checks.claim: Key: this carrying of pollen is pollination
checks.note: 'Pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther of a flower to the stigma...'; 'successful pollination is a prerequisite for seed and fruit formation'.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Germination' (a seed sprouting), 'Seed dispersal' (spreading finished seeds), 'Photosynthesis' (making food from light)
checks.note: None is defensible for moving pollen between flowers.

checks.claim: Context: pollen is made by the flower's stamens
checks.note: Stamen = filament + anther; pollen develops in the anther's microsporangia. Optional precision: pollination is pollen's journey to the same or another flower (self-pollination counts); 'to another flower' is true for this bee scenario.

checks.claim: Context: bees, butterflies, birds, bats and the wind all carry pollen
checks.note: Vectors listed: 'wind, water, birds, insects, butterflies, bats, and other animals'.

checks.claim: Key: an acorn is botanically a fruit
checks.note: 'the fruit of oak trees in the genus Quercus'; 'the nut, botanically classified as an achene fruit'. Wikipedia Nut (fruit): 'A nut is a fruit consisting of a hard or tough nutshell protecting a single seed'; acorns listed among 'true nuts'.

checks.claim: Stem: an acorn grows from one of the oak's tiny flowers
checks.note: 'tiny reddish-green pistillate flowers'; the ovary becomes the acorn's body, other flower parts the cap.

checks.claim: Stem: inside its hard shell lies a seed
checks.note: 'a single seed enclosed within a hard, woody shell'.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'A cone' (conifers bear naked seeds on cones; oaks are flowering plants)
checks.note: 'woody cones that bear naked seeds not enclosed in an ovary'.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'A bud' and 'A bulb'
checks.note: An acorn is the mature ovary holding a seed; neither a bud nor an underground storage bulb.

checks.claim: Context: a fruit grows from a flower and holds and protects its seeds; maple helicopters are fruits
checks.note: Samara: 'a dry, indehiscent fruit containing a single seed surrounded by a wing-like structure'; maples' called 'helicopter seeds'. Grokipedia Fruit: fruits 'protect the seeds and aid in their dispersal'.

checks.claim: Context: pines have no flowers, so a pine cone holds seeds but is not a fruit
checks.note: Conifers 'lack these features' (flowers and enclosed seeds), 'with their ovules borne openly on cone scales'.

checks.claim: Key: a coconut floats (air in its husk) and ocean currents carry it to far shores
checks.note: 'buoyancy, derived from air cavities in the husk'; Grokipedia Seed dispersal: 'thick, fibrous pericarp that traps air, enabling it to float for months'. Wikipedia Coconut: 'The fruit is adapted for ocean dispersal.'

checks.claim: Context: the seed inside stays alive for months at sea
checks.note: 'viability in seawater for up to 110-120 days'. Oxford Plants 400 (https://herbaria.plants.ox.ac.uk/bol/plants400/Profiles/cd/Cocos): 'remain viable only for about 110 days'. Edmondson (1941, Bishop Museum), as reported by Cadee in PALMS 2008: 10 of 15 coconuts could still develop after floating up to 110 days.

checks.claim: Does a sea-carried coconut then sprout on a new shore?
checks.note: Harries and Clement 2014 (Annals of Botany): waves carry nuts onto bare coral rock where 'seednuts must germinate, root and establish'; Oxford Plants 400: 'Coconuts are great maritime voyagers and coastal colonizers'; 'cast on to desert island shores... coconut seeds must germinate and root'. Caution for future edits: drift models show coconuts could not have crossed the whole Pacific unaided (Wikipedia Coconut; Ward and Brookfield 1992), and humans spread much of the crop, so never claim coconuts spread around the world by floating. The present wording ('far shores', 'for months') is safe.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'A dandelion seed' (rides the wind on a parachute-like pappus)
checks.note: Pappus 'acts as a parachute to increase drag'; not a sea drifter.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'A prickly burr' (hooks onto fur)
checks.note: 'hooks, barbs, or hairs that latch onto fur'.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'A maple helicopter' (spins on the wind)
checks.note: Spinning slows the fall so the wind carries it farther from the tree; not a sea drifter.

checks.claim: Stem: a soaked bean swells and its skin splits before the young plant grows out
checks.note: 'the seed absorbs water through its coat, initiating imbibition, which swells and softens the seed coat'. Beans sprout on a damp towel without soil (NSTA Needs of Seeds: 'Seeds can sprout without soil as long as they have a source of moisture').

checks.claim: Key: the root (radicle) comes out first
checks.note: 'the radicle (primary root) protrudes first through the seed coat, followed by the shoot and cotyledons'. Wikipedia Radicle: 'the first part of a seedling to emerge from the seed'. Bean-specific: David Darling encyclopedia's bean sequence (https://www.daviddarling.info/encyclopedia/G/germination.html): 'The radicle has broken through the testa and is growing downward', then the plumule grows upward. True of beans and of most seeds; rare exceptions (e.g. rice under water, coleoptile first) do not touch a bean on a towel.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'The stem', 'The leaves', 'The bud' (the shoot and its leaves follow the root)
checks.note: The hypocotyl (young stem) elongates and the plumule (shoot bud with first leaves) rises only after the radicle has emerged.

checks.claim: Context: the root grows down, holds the seedling and takes in water; the shoot then pushes up toward the light
checks.note: Radicle grows 'downward in the soil' and draws water and minerals.

checks.claim: Stem: a soaked bean slips its thin skin and splits into two thick halves with a tiny plant between them
checks.note: Seed = embryo + stored food (endosperm or cotyledons) + protective seed coat; 'Cotyledons, the embryonic leaves, attach laterally to the axis'. (Botanically the cotyledons are part of the embryo; calling the axis 'a tiny plant tucked between them' is the standard grade-5 simplification.)

checks.claim: Key: the two halves (cotyledons) feed the young plant as it starts to grow
checks.note: 'Non-endospermic seeds, prevalent in dicots such as beans and peas, rely on enlarged cotyledons for stored nutrients'. Grokipedia Germination: 'the two cotyledons function as primary storage organs'.

checks.claim: Context: the food was stored there by the parent plant and feeds the seedling until it can make its own food in the light
checks.note: 'This food was made by the parent plant and stored in seeds for later use by the embryo'. Wikipedia Seedling: 'Until this stage, the seedling lives off the energy reserves stored in the seed'.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Hold air for it to breathe'
checks.note: Seeds take air from around them ('Air is necessary for seeds to respire'); the cotyledons are solid food stores, not air stores.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Grow into its first roots'
checks.note: The root grows from the radicle of the embryonic axis, not from the cotyledons.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Take in water from the soil'
checks.note: Water enters through the seed coat during imbibition and later through the root; taking in soil water is not the cotyledons' job. (The cotyledons do swell with water during soaking, but that is not something they do for the young plant.)

checks.claim: Context: the seed coat protects it; the root grows from the tiny plant itself
checks.note: Seed coat 'protecting the embryo from physical damage and pathogen ingress'.

checks.claim: Key: animals eat the berries and spread the seeds
checks.note: Endozoochory: animals 'consume fruits containing seeds, which pass through the digestive tract and are excreted intact'. Grokipedia Fruit: fleshy fruits 'attract vertebrates'; birds or mammals 'consume berries and excrete viable seeds elsewhere'.

checks.claim: Context: seeds pass through unharmed, drop out in droppings, often far from the parent plant
checks.note: Some seeds are destroyed by some seed-eating birds, but the general statement holds for fruit-eaters.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Bees feed on them and carry their pollen'
checks.note: Pollen is made by flowers' anthers; a ripe berry has no pollen to carry.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'They hold water for the dry summer' and 'They keep the seeds warm in winter'
checks.note: A fruit's roles are to protect the seeds and aid their dispersal; neither choice is a documented job of a berry.

checks.claim: Context: pollen comes from flowers, and a berry grows only after its flower has been pollinated
checks.note: Fruit 'develops after fertilization'. Exception: parthenocarpic fruits form without fertilization (https://grokipedia.com/page/Parthenocarpy), but they are seedless or nearly so; for the stem's seed-holding berries the statement is true. Optional tightening: 'a berry with seeds grows only after its flower has been pollinated'.

unit_notes: All nine questions check out. The coconut question is safe as worded (it floats, currents carry it to far shores, the seed lives about 110-120 days, and drifted nuts do germinate on bare shores per Harries and Clement 2014 and Oxford Plants 400), but future edits must not claim coconuts spread around the world by drift: drift models show the Pacific was not crossed unaided and humans spread much of the crop. Two optional precision tweaks, not errors: pollination is pollen's move to the same or another flower (self-pollination counts); and a berry 'with seeds' grows only after pollination (seedless parthenocarpic fruits are the exception).
